newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels cheered as peace returns to Kinshasa.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels cheered as peace returns to Kinshasa.

text.p: KINSHASA, May 18, Reuter - Laurent Kabila's rebel Alliance marched triumphantly through Zaire's capital Kinshasa on Sunday, cheered by onlookers and urged by world powers to form a broad-based government as a bridge to elections.

Residents reported isolated resistance from loyalist soldiers, one day after the rebels entered the capital. Bodies of soldiers and civilians killed in overnight shootouts with rebels littered Kinshasa neighbourhoods.

However, the United States and Britain, among Western nations with troops on standby in Congo to evacuate foreigners from Zaire, said they were scaling back their operation as peace returned to Kinshasa.

The fate and whereabouts of ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko, 66 and suffering from prostate cancer, remained uncertain. A spokesman for the rebels vowed they would hunt him and his clan down "wherever he goes".
"With us, he will never be in peace. Wherever he goes, we will find him," Zamba Afri Kounyen, spokesman in France for the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL), said.
Rebel leader Kabila, 56, sent a delegation to Kinshasa from the southeastern city of Lubumbashi on Sunday.
"I am going to contact all my compatriots without exception. There are parties, civil organisations, everyone," Deogratius Bugera, Secretary-General of the Alliance, told Reuters.
Bugera would not say when Kabila would visit Kinshasa.

Mobutu's whereabouts were unclear. A security official in Morocco said he had arrived there. In Paris, a family friend said Mobutu was still in his ancestral home in Gdabolite northern Zaire, where he fled on Friday.

Liechtenstein, responding to French news reports that Mobutu might travel there, said he would not be welcome. Neighbouring Switzerland, where Mobutu had cancer surgery in August, said on Saturday it would most likely reject any visa request from him.
Fugitive members of Mobutu's clan, including his soldier son Kongolo, cooled their heels across the river from Kinshasa as reluctant host Congo tried to find countries to take them.
Kabila's forces, who took up arms in October, marched into the government and diplomatic quarters on Sunday, after a night of sporadic shooting in areas not yet under their control.
In its first broadcast over national radio in Kinshasa, the rebels had ordered all government troops to report by Sunday and warned looters they would be severely punished.
One witness saw 40 bodies collected from different neighbourhoods in one hour on Sunday, most of them soldiers who went on a last-minute looting spree on Saturday night.
South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki arrived at rebel headquarters in Lubumbashi to become the first foreign dignitary to meet Kabila since he proclaimed himself head of state.
The African National Congress formally congratulated Kabila and his Alliance and said the absence of major bloodshed was a tribute to South African President Nelson Mandela's mediation.
The United States, former colonial power Belgium, France, one of Mobutu's last friends, and Germany reacted to Kabila's victory by calling for a broad-based government and elections.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, speaking in Moscow, echoed that message and urged Kabila to respect the "choice and voice" of the Zairean people.

The Organisation of African Unity urged reconciliation. "The people of Congo-Zaire have great expectations. So does Africa." Kenya, Tanzania and Rwanda, said they would work with a new government under Kabila.

Pope John Paul called for the plight of Rwandan Hutu refugees not to be overlooked. France, a long-time Mobutu ally, acknowleded Zaire's shift of power and urged the Alliance to allow a U.N. probe of reports that rebels massacred refugees.
A U.N. airlift of the Hutus home to Rwanda passed the 30,000 mark on Sunday but aid officials said refugees were still dying in their dozens both in Zaire and Rwanda.
In Kinshasa, national television, under new management, rang the changes by denouncing Mobutu as a dictator.

Within hours of Mobutu being ousted, Switzerland blocked all assets he and his family may have there. Swiss media have speculated that he may have some $4 billion stashed in the neutral Alpine haven. Bankers there were sceptical of this.
